BXL-2425-00006-v4.headline: Push back to 1 January 2027 the deadline forcing Brussels taxis to buy zero-emission (electric/hydrogen) vehicles — a two-year delay from the 1 January 2025 date set by decree.
BXL-2425-00006-v4.proposed_by: Jamal Ikazban, Ahmed Laaouej, Ibrahim Dönmez, Leila Agic, Amin El Boujdaini, Sevket Temiz, Aline Godfrin, Sadik Köksal, David Weytsman, Loubna Azghoud (PS, MR e.a.)
BXL-2425-00006-v4.source_brief:
A regional decree currently requires Brussels taxis to switch to zero-emission vehicles when they renew their licence, with the obligation biting from **1 January 2025**. This ordinance moves that deadline to **1 January 2027**, giving the sector two more years before the rule applies.

- **Who it touches:** about **700 taxis** hit the seven-year age limit and would have to be replaced by emission-free vehicles by end-2025; the active fleet is **3,250**, of which only **240** are already electric.
- **The cost argument:** a thermal taxi can be bought for around **€30,000**, while a comparable-capacity electric one runs two to three times more (one group cited **€60,000–80,000**); drivers are mostly small self-employed operators who receive no public purchase subsidy in Brussels.
- **The counter-argument:** an official task force judged the public charging network adequate, and opponents warn that fine particles and CO2 from road traffic harm residents' lungs — delaying the switch keeps higher-emitting cars on the road two more years.
- **The rub:** is a two-year reprieve a fair fix for a struggling sector facing infrastructure gaps, or a retreat from air-quality and climate commitments without a contradictory hearing of the experts?
deep_facts: The text sets at **1 January 2027** the deadline for taxi services to acquire zero-emission vehicles; it is the ordinance route (A-38), given priority over a competing resolution (A-20) under the hierarchy-of-norms principle, which thereby became without object (CRI, 6 Dec 2024).

The obligation originally applied from **1 January 2025** under an arrêté; the proposers present the two-year postponement as necessary for a sector facing high fixed costs, a shortage of fast charging points, and insufficient electric-vehicle range (CRI, 6 Dec 2024).

The obligation does not hit all taxis at once: a driver is bound only at **renewal of their authorisation**. Near **700 vehicles** reach the seven-year age limit and would have to be replaced by zero-emission vehicles by end-2025 (CRI, 6 Dec 2024).

Fleet figures cited: roughly **240 electric taxis** are already running out of a total of **3,250** active taxis in the Region; some operators installed charging points or solar panels with no public aid (CRI, 6 Dec 2024).

Price figures cited: a vehicle suitable for paid passenger transport can be acquired for about **€30,000**, whereas a good-capacity electric vehicle 'often costs double, even triple' that amount; Team Fouad Ahidar cited a purchase cost of **€60,000 to €80,000** as a brake on electrification (CRI, 6 Dec 2024).

A government condition stated the obligation could apply only if the Region had a sufficient number of charging points by 2025. In September, the electric-charging-points task force presented a study to the government concluding the network was adapted to the sector's needs (CRI, 6 Dec 2024).

Proposers contest that study: they say it was done without the sector's collaboration, relies on manufacturers' range data (range drops sharply with AC/heating), assumes most drivers charge at night, and that Belgian public-charging tariffs are among Europe's highest (third for slow charging, behind Croatia and Denmark, per a Transport & Mobility Leuven study) (CRI, 6 Dec 2024).

Bruxelles Mobilité took position in the dossier asking to postpone the obligation set for 1 January 2025, citing inadequate and insufficient electrical infrastructure; there are no hydrogen stations in the Region and no charging points exclusively reserved for taxis (CRI, 6 Dec 2024).

Positions stated in committee (26 Nov): PS, MR, PTB, N-VA and Team Fouad Ahidar favourable to the postponement; Les Engagés, Groen and Ecolo opposed; DéFI favoured a one-year rather than two-year delay (CRI, 6 Dec 2024).

Amendments tabled: a PTB amendment for an intermediate review in September 2026 to verify accompanying measures and fast-charging deployment; a DéFI amendment for a one-year postponement (CRI, 6 Dec 2024).

Les Engagés argued the arrêté of 6 October 2022 already allowed a postponement if charging infrastructure was deemed insufficient, but the task force gave a favourable opinion on the initial measure; they proposed either auditioning the task force or rejecting the text and following the initial deadline (CRI, 6 Dec 2024).

Ecolo argued the existing **7,000 charging points** suffice and that electrification is profitable long-term via lower operating costs; Groen stressed fine-particle harm to residents with pulmonary/respiratory conditions (CRI, 6 Dec 2024).

Procedural sequence: two amendments to Article 2 were tabled, followed by Article 2 non-amended and then the ensemble; once adopted, the ordinance is to be submitted to the government for sanction (CRI, 6 Dec 2024).

The seven-year age limit on taxis is cited as a guarantee that thermal vehicles in service are modern and low-emitting; the sector states it is not against decarbonisation but judged the 1 January 2025 date unworkable (CRI, 6 Dec 2024).
deep_lectura: **Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*

The split is not left-vs-right but environment-vs-livelihood: a PS–MR–PTB–N-VA bloc lined up behind the sector, while the green family (Ecolo, Groen) plus Les Engagés held the air-quality line — an unusual cross-ideological coalition that signals taxi-driver constituencies weigh heavily across parties.

Choosing the ordinance over the resolution, and the choice on the PTB 'review in 2026' and the DéFI 'one year' amendments, decides whether the delay is a clean two years or a conditional, checkpointed one — the unconditional reprieve is what the sector wanted and what opponents most distrust.

Much of the floor speech attacks the task force study's methodology; functionally this pre-empts the 'the network is ready' objection, since if the official adequacy finding stands, the legal basis for delay (insufficient infrastructure) weakens.
The framing of taxis as small self-employed operators from working-class neighbourhoods reframes an emissions question as a social-equity one, raising the political cost of voting against the delay.
BXL-2425-00006-v4.raw_fr: Proposition d'ordonnance visant à fixer au 1er janvier 2027 l'échéance, pour les services de taxis, d'acquérir des véhicules zéro émission. Les signataires présentent ce report de deux ans comme nécessaire pour un secteur confronté à des coûts fixes élevés, un manque de bornes de recharge rapide et une autonomie insuffisante des véhicules électriques. Près de 700 véhicules atteindront la limite d'âge de sept ans et devraient être remplacés d'ici fin 2025.

BXL-2425-00006-v5.headline: Keep taxing public buildings used for general-interest missions unless the law expressly exempts them — closing a loophole that could have quietly spread tax exemptions from 2025.
BXL-2425-00006-v5.proposed_by: Imane Belguenani (Open Vld), Stijn Bex, Jonathan de Patoul (DéFI)
BXL-2425-00006-v5.source_brief:
When the Region's Code of Public Finances was overhauled in April 2024, its Article 175 — due to take effect on **1 January 2025** — turned out to be open to several readings, one of which could have broadened tax exemptions for public-domain property. This ordinance rewrites it to state plainly that such property is taxable unless an exemption is expressly granted.

- **What is at stake:** the Region's ability to keep taxing buildings on the public and private domain; the change is presented as preserving regional tax revenue and avoiding losses of fiscal receipts in 2025.
- **The legal anchor:** it codifies settled **Court of Cassation** case-law (public-domain goods exempt from *communal* taxes only) and aligns with the **Conseil d'État** opinion given in early 2024; proposers stress it changes nothing in current policy and never intended a general exemption regime.
- **The rub:** a 'merely technical' clarification that nonetheless decides whether public-interest property can be broadly shielded from regional tax — a precaution worth locking in, or a fix being rushed through just before the article takes effect?
deep_facts: The proposition modifies the ordinance of 4 April 2024 bearing the Code of Public Finances of the Brussels-Capital Region, specifically clarifying **Article 175**, whose entry into force is set at **1 January 2025** (CRI, 6 Dec 2024).

After publication of the new code in the Moniteur belge, several interpretations of Article 175 appeared possible; the stated object is to specify, unambiguously, that all goods of the public and private domain assigned to general-interest missions are subject to regional taxes and levies, **save express derogation** (CRI, 6 Dec 2024).
Scope: the rule concerns the domanial goods of the Region as well as those of other public entities (CRI, 6 Dec 2024).

The clarification was introduced via an amendment in committee; it is described as deleting a provision that merely confirmed the established Court of Cassation case-law under which public-domain goods are exempt from **communal** taxes (CRI, 6 Dec 2024).

Stated rationale: when the ordinance was approved in 2024 there was no intention to institute a general tax-exemption regime that would prevent the Region from taxing buildings; the change aims to secure the legal certainty of the Region's fiscal revenue and avoid losses or risk of losses of fiscal receipts in 2025 (CRI, 6 Dec 2024).
The modification is stated to conform to the initial opinion rendered by the **Conseil d'État** in early 2024 on the draft new code (CRI, 6 Dec 2024).

Process: examined by the Finance and General Affairs committee on **2 December 2024**; in plenary, Articles 1, 2 and 3 were taken without observation before the vote on the ensemble (CRI, 6 Dec 2024).
The text is to be submitted to the government for sanction (CRI, 6 Dec 2024).
deep_lectura: **Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*

Despite the 'technical' label, the item is a revenue-protection move: left unfixed, the ambiguous Article 175 risked being read as a broad exemption, which would have eroded the Region's tax base — so the vote is effectively for or against keeping public-interest property taxable.

The cross-bench authorship (Open Vld, DéFI) suggests broad consensus that this is housekeeping rather than a contested policy choice; any reservations are likely to read as concerns about substance-by-amendment or timing rather than opposition to the principle.

Acting before the article's 1 January 2025 entry into force is the point: fixing it after the fact would have meant litigating exemption claims, so the urgency is about pre-empting interpretation disputes, not changing policy direction.
BXL-2425-00006-v5.raw_fr: Proposition d'ordonnance modifiant l'ordonnance du 4 avril 2024 portant le Code des finances publiques de la Région de Bruxelles-Capitale, afin de clarifier l'article 175. Elle précise, sans ambiguïté, que tous les biens du domaine public et privé affectés à des missions d'intérêt général sont bien soumis aux taxes et impôts régionaux, sauf dérogation expresse, préservant ainsi les recettes fiscales de la Région.
